candidato.titulo: New strategy may target common cancer driver with minimal side effects
candidato.resumo: Researchers have found a surprisingly common vulnerability in a broad variety of cancers and have begun designing drug compounds to exploit it, in a study led by investigators at Weill Cornell Medicine. The findings suggest the possibility of a potent, low-side-effect treatment that could benefit many patients with colorectal, breast and other cancer types.

texto_fonte:
New strategy may target common cancer driver with minimal side effects
Researchers have found a surprisingly common vulnerability in a broad variety of cancers and have begun designing drug compounds to exploit it, in a study led by investigators at Weill Cornell Medicine. The findings suggest the possibility of a potent, low-side-effect treatment that could benefit many patients with colorectal, breast and other cancer types.
The new strategy targets a signaling pathway called the WNT pathway, whose hyperactivity is common in cancers and boosts malignancy through multiple mechanisms. Targeting WNT signaling without harming normal cells has been notoriously difficult.
However, in the study, which appears in Nature Chemical Biology, the researchers found that many cancer cells are deficient in one of two redundant WNT-supporting enzymes. They showed that selectively targeting the remaining one reduces WNT signaling in such cells with no apparent effect on healthy cells. The researchers demonstrated the strategy successfully in early preclinical experiments with a selective enzyme inhibitor they developed.
"There's still a lot of work to be done, but so far this looks like a rare example of being able to use tumor cells' genetics to target them while sparing normal cells," said study senior author Dr. Lukas Dow, professor of biochemistry in medicine and a member of the Sandra and Edward Meyer Cancer Center at Weill Cornell Medicine.
The study's first author was Dr. Jill Zimmerman, a Weill Cornell Graduate School of Medical Sciences doctoral student in the Dow Lab during the study.
A missing enzyme exposes cancer cells
WNT pathway hyperactivity is seen in almost all colorectal cancers, more than half of breast cancers and substantial proportions of liver, lung, prostate, skin, bone and gynecologic cancers. One anti-WNT strategy has been to target a pair of WNT-supporting "tankyrase" enzymes called TNKS1 and TNKS2. But inhibiting these enzymes can harm healthy cells too, and experimental tankyrase inhibitors have had dose-limiting side effects in initial clinical trials.
Several years ago, however, Dow and his team discovered a common vulnerability in WNT-driven cancers that had been hiding in plain sight.
"We stumbled across this by accident," Dow said. "We were knocking down TNKS1 and TNKS2 independently, to understand how their biological roles might differ, and we noticed that in some cancer cells, we needed to knock down only TNKS2 to see an effect on WNT signaling."
As they develop, most cancers undergo large-scale DNA deletions, and the researchers realized that one of the most common of these happens to delete the gene for TNKS1. That in itself doesn't harm the cancer cells, since TNKS2 is still present and serves the same function. But it gives these cancerous cells a selective vulnerability to the loss of TNKS2—so that a drug inhibiting just TNKS2 could hobble or kill those cancerous cells while sparing healthy, TNKS1-containing cells.
Designing a selective TNKS2 inhibitor
The team confirmed the viability of the concept using genetic techniques to suppress TNKS2 selectively, then set out to develop a drug molecule that could do the same thing.
Devising a TNKS2 inhibitor that would have little effect on TNKS1 was a real challenge, given that the active sites of TNKS1 and TNKS2 are virtually identical. But with collaborating computational and medicinal chemists, the team ultimately was able to come up with an effective design based on what was known about the slightly different structures of the two enzymes.
Screening compounds made according to this design strategy yielded one that inhibits TNKS2 about 30 times more than TNKS1. In lab dish tests, the compound suppressed the growth of cancer cells that had partial or full TNKS1 loss, but did not affect the growth of cells containing a normal amount of TNKS1.
Toward a drug ready for testing
The Dow lab now hopes to develop a next-generation compound that will have better drug-like properties using detailed structural models of TNKS1 and TNKS2 developed late in the study. If such a compound performs well in full preclinical tests, the researchers hope to take it into clinical trials.
"Targeting the WNT pathway in cancer without side effects has been a challenge for decades now, but we're aiming to change that," Dow said.
Publication details
Zimmerman, J., et al. A selective TNKS2 inhibitor for tumor-restricted WNT suppression. Nature Chemical Biology (2026). doi.org/10.1038/s41589-026-02358-z
Journal information: Nature Chemical Biology

candidato.titulo: A CRISPR gene boost reduces seizures and strengthens muscles in mice
candidato.resumo: Some genetic diseases leave cells without a crucial protein. One possible treatment is to persuade genes already inside those cells to work harder, but the necessary machinery can be difficult to deliver, especially when researchers want to target several genes at once. A new compact CRISPR system devised by Hainan Zhang of the Shanghai Institute of Materia Medica, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and colleagues fits those instructions into a single viral delivery package.

texto_fonte:
A CRISPR gene boost reduces seizures and strengthens muscles in mice
Andrew Zinin
Author
Some genetic diseases leave cells without a crucial protein. One possible treatment is to persuade genes already inside those cells to work harder, but the necessary machinery can be difficult to deliver, especially when researchers want to target several genes at once. A new compact CRISPR system devised by Hainan Zhang of the Shanghai Institute of Materia Medica, Chinese Academy of Sciences, and colleagues fits those instructions into a single viral delivery package.
In separate mouse experiments, the treatment reduced seizures and prevented early deaths in a model of Dravet syndrome, and it produced lasting improvements in muscle function in a model of Duchenne muscular dystrophy.
These results, published in Nature Biotechnology, suggest that turning up helpful genes rather than repairing mutations may be a better way to influence cell behavior in genetic diseases.
Making room for more instructions
The system uses CRISPR activation, which directs molecular machinery to a gene's control region to increase its activity without cutting the DNA. But delivering that machinery creates a packaging problem because adeno-associated viruses, which are used to carry genetic instructions into cells, have limited cargo space. The package must incorporate both the protein that helps activate genes and the RNA guides that direct it to the right places.
The researchers built their system around Cas12m, a small CRISPR protein that can also cut a chain of RNA guides into separate working pieces inside a cell. In this way, several guides can share one compact set of instructions.
After engineering the protein and its accompanying components, the team created a platform called smCRISPRa that allows multiple guides to focus its activity on one gene or distribute it across several. In one demonstration, a single viral vector carried eight guides that increased the activity of six genes in mouse brain and muscle tissues.
Boosting a working gene—or recruiting a substitute
In the Dravet syndrome model, the mice had only one functional copy of Scn1a, leaving them without a protein needed for normal brain signaling. The researchers injected the viral delivery package into fluid-filled spaces in the brains of newborn mice.
The treatment raised protein levels to normal or higher and reduced seizures. All 31 treated mice survived the roughly 100-day observation period, compared with about 60% of 30 disease-model mice that were given a control injection.
To treat Duchenne muscular dystrophy, the team pursued a different solution. The disease involves loss of dystrophin, which helps protect muscle cells, so the researchers boosted utrophin, a related protein that can perform some of dystrophin's functions.
Two-week-old mice received the treatment intravenously. They were able to grip more strongly, stayed longer on a rotating rod, and they resisted muscle fatigue better than the control mice. The benefits persisted six months after treatment, when testing showed that grip strength and rotating-rod performance were similar to those of healthy mice.
A separate experiment combined utrophin activation with the activation of a gene involved in increasing muscle mass. That therapy produced modest additional benefits, suggesting that extra cargo capacity could support combinations of targets.
Further testing is needed across disease models and doses, and because both main disease experiments were conducted on very young mice, the safety of altering several genes' activity requires closer scrutiny. As the authors write, "Clinical translation requires comprehensive off-target evaluation" and checking for unintended effects beyond the intended targets.
Yet the versatile, all-in-one strategy of the smCRISPRa platform represents a promising pathway for the treatment of various genetic disorders. The compact package gives researchers room to test combinations that could help cells in complementary ways: producing more of an available protein, recruiting a substitute or strengthening another part of the same tissue.

We rely on readers like you to keep independent science journalism alive. If this reporting matters to you, please consider a donation (especially monthly). You'll get an ad-free account as a thank-you.

candidato.titulo: A Meta quer entrar na sua casa, agora com um robô humanoide
candidato.resumo: Criado em parceria com a chinesa Fourier, robô humanoide da Meta teria 1,5 de altura e tela na cabeça que mostra expressões faciais. A Meta quer entrar na sua casa, agora com um robô humanoide

texto_fonte:
Resumo
- A Meta está desenvolvendo um robô humanoide chamado Max, com aproximadamente 1,5 metro de altura e um visor na cabeça capaz de mostrar expressões faciais.
- O robô está sendo desenvolvido em parceria com a Fourier, uma startup chinesa especializada em robótica, e já está em fase avançada de desenvolvimento.
- Aparentemente, o Max é projetado para interagir com humanos, podendo ser direcionado a tarefas específicas em ambientes como lares, espaços públicos ou escritórios.
Quando o assunto é robô humanoide, talvez você se lembre imediatamente da Boston Dynamics. Mas, surpreendentemente, a Meta também está trabalhando em um projeto do tipo: trata-se de um robô de codinome Max, aproximadamente 1,5 metro de altura e um visor na cabeça capaz de mostrar expressões faciais.
Pelo menos é o que conta o site The Information, citando fontes próximas à Meta familiarizadas com o projeto. As mesmas fontes dão conta de que a turma de Mark Zuckerberg não está sozinha nessa empreitada: o robô estaria sendo desenvolvido em parceria com a Fourier, uma startup chinesa especializada em robótica.
Se os burburinhos estiverem corretos, o robô já está em fase avançada de desenvolvimento. Funcionários da Meta teriam passado cerca de dois meses na China trabalhando junto com a Fourier no projeto e, após esse período, viram um robô de 1,5 m de altura, 48 quilos e mãos com cinco dedos cada ganhar forma.
O fato de o Max ter um visor na cabeça que o permite mostrar expressões faciais deixa claro que o robô está sendo desenvolvido para interagir com humanos. Nesse sentido, o robô poderá ser direcionado à execução de tarefas específicas do lar, de ambientes públicos ou de escritórios, presumivelmente.
Reforça a possibilidade de o robô ser projetado para o convívio com os humanos a capacidade de suas mãos de pegar pequenos objetos, a presença de cinco alto-falantes em seu corpo e o fato de o Max ser baseado no Jetson AGX Thor, plataforma da Nvidia projetada para viabilizar principalmente projetos de robôs humanoides.
Ainda de acordo com os burburinhos, o projeto avança em ritmo acelerado, tanto que um segundo protótipo do robô já está a caminho: o Max 2, como vem sendo chamado, terá a parte superior do seu corpo redesenhada, mãos aprimoradas e sensores que o permitem subir escadas.
Note, porém, que nenhuma imagem do Max foi divulgada até o momento (a foto abaixo, ilustrativa, mostra os robôs da Fourier).
Quando a Meta lançará o Max?
Ninguém sabe ao certo. Procurada para comentar o assunto, a companhia disse apenas que o Max é um projeto interno, razão pela qual os seus objetivos com esse robô não estão claros.
No fim das contas, é possível que o Max sirva de ponto de partida para o desenvolvimento de tecnologias de robótica ou de outros robôs. Ao que tudo indica, a Meta quer entrar de vez no segmento de robôs humanoides. Não por acaso, a companhia adquiriu, em maio deste ano, a Assured Robot Intelligence (ARI), uma startup focada justamente nesse tipo de robótica, como lembra o Engadget.

texto_fonte:
ChatGPT vai juntar conversas e agentes de IA no mesmo lugar do app
Por André Lourenti Magalhães |
A OpenAI vai unificar as abas “Chat” e “Work” no ChatGPT. Dessa forma, a conversa padrão e o agente de IA do Work poderão ser acessados na mesma caixa de prompt, sem a necessidade de alternar entre os modos na tela inicial.
A empresa começou a informar aos assinantes dos planos pagos do ChatGPT sobre a mudança, que será testada com um grupo limitado de contas a partir das próximas semanas. A divisão entre abas existe na versão web e nos aplicativos para computadores e celulares.
O ajuste simplifica a experiência de uso, visto que uma tarefa pode conversar no chat padrão e depois ser encaminhada para o agente do Work. “Isso vai permitir avançar da exploração de uma ideia até a execução pelo ChatGPT, tudo no mesmo lugar”, explica a empresa em comunicado.
O ChatGPT Work foi lançado pela OpenAI em julho e funciona como um agente autônomo para executar diferentes tarefas. A ferramenta pode acessar documentos no computador, combinar ações entre apps — o usuário delega as funções e acompanha todo o processo, sempre com a opção de intervir no meio do caminho.
O que muda no Codex?
O assistente de programação Codex ainda vai funcionar de forma separada, mas vai consumir tokens de forma conjunta com o ChatGPT. Ou seja, prompts feitos no chat e no agente de código vão consumir os mesmos limites de uso.
A empresa afirma que o ajuste não deve impactar a maioria das pessoas, mas um grupo seleto pode ter que aumentar o controle do consumo de IA.

texto_fonte:
There's a brilliant discount on a high-spec gaming PC right now that'll net you 4K-ready performance. Newegg has dropped the price on this ABS Stratos II Aqua gaming PC to $2,549.99 right now, netting you a PC with a 24-core Intel CPU and one of Nvidia's best GPUs, along with a $450 saving. This discount is covered by Newegg's Black Friday price protection, so if the price drops again in the big sale, you'll get a refund for the difference.
Newegg owns the ABS brand, so this isn't a knock-off you're getting. It has a good set of specs for a rig that'll handle 4K gaming, shipping with an Intel Core i9-14900KF processor, along with a current-gen Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070 Ti GPU, 32GB of DDR5-6400 memory, and 2TB of SSD storage. Given the current market conditions, these are good specs to find at this price point.
The ABS Strators II Aqua gaming PC comes with a 24-core Intel Core i9-14900KF CPU, an Nvidia GeForce GeForce RTX 5070 Ti graphics card, a 2TB NVMe SSD with Gen 4 speeds, and 32GB of DDR5-6400 RAM. This is a high-end gaming PC that'll handle games at 4K.
With a machine like this, you're able to ditch 1080p completely. The RTX 5070 Ti is a graphics card that has more than enough performance for gaming at 1440p and 4K, especially if you're able to tweak your graphics settings for the most performing games. It's a good option for a mid-tier build, and it comes with 8,960 CUDA cores, along with 16GB of GDDR7 VRAM.
As this Blackwell GPU is one of Nvidia's latest, you've got fully Nvidia DLSS support included. That includes multi-frame generation, which will give you an AI-generated frame rate boost in any really intensive games, especially at 4K, to make them playable.
As for the CPU, the Intel Core i9-14900KF CPU continues to be a popular choice for gaming PCs at this price point, and despite being a little older, it still packs a punch. You're getting 24 cores here, of which eight are performance cores that will give your machine the best gaming performance. The other 16 are efficiency cores, which are great for multi-threaded tasks. You'll be able to push this CPU's clock up to a massive 6 GHz, too.
Our CPU benchmarks still have a place for the i9-14900K, the same CPU but with an integrated GPU that the 14900KF here lacks. It continues to be one of the best-performing processors on sale for gamers if you're not going all-in with an AMD X3D build.
There are no compromises to be found elsewhere in this rig. 32GB of G.Skill Ripjaws M5 Neo (2 x 16GB) DDR5-6000 memory is included here, letting you leave the slower speeds of DDR4 behind. A 2TB Team Group NV5000 SSD is also included in this ABS build, so you'll have space for a good collection of games, with the NV5000 offering Gen 4 speeds.
Prices continue to rise in the PC hardware market, but the $450 discount on this ABS Stratos II Aqua rig, down to $2,549.99, is a good one. You're also able to take advantage of Newegg's Black Friday price guarantee, so if this PC drops down in price over Black Friday, you'll be able to claim back the difference. If you need a new 4K gaming PC on a budget, you'll want to pick up a rig like this one.

candidato.titulo: James Webb Space Telescope uncovers new clues about the origins of 'interstellar invader' comet 3I/ATLAS
candidato.resumo: The findings are another clue towards understanding the origins of 3I/ATLAS and the planet-forming conditions around other stars.

texto_fonte:
Using the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), scientists have found that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was built from tiny grains of ice mixed with dust that are quite different from the solar system’s comets.
These ice grains do, however, bear striking similarities to some icy bodies located at the edge of the solar system, beyond the orbit of Neptune, so-called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs).
3I/ATLAS was discovered entering the solar system in the summer of 2025. It was only the third object found entering the solar system from farther afield in the Milky Way after 1I/'Oumuamua, seen in 2017, and 2I/Borisov, detected in 2019. This meant the interstellar comet offered a rare chance to glimpse the conditions under which such bodies form in other star systems. Thus, the JWST was quickly on the trail of 3I/ATLAS.
"We designed [JWST] to be ready the moment an active interstellar comet was found and to follow it over time," Martin Cordiner of NASA’s Goddard Space Flight Center and the Catholic University of America said in a statement.
Cordiner leads the JWST program to study objects such as 3I/ATLAS, and he is a co-author on a new research paper describing some of the findings.
The unclear origins of 3I/ATLAS
Researchers know that 3I/ATLAS wasn't born in the solar system, but nobody knows around which star 3I/ATLAS formed. What scientists are more sure of is the fact that this interstellar comet was produced within a planet-forming disk of gas and dust around a young star, possibly as long ago as 10 to 12 billion years. That's over twice the age of our solar system. It was then ejected from its home system somehow and left to wander interstellar space before encountering our solar system.
Like the familiar comets in our solar system, 3I/ATLAS is composed of grains of ice less than a micron – a millionth of a meter – in size. When the surface of the comet is warmed by the sun, gas erupts outwards, carrying ice grains into the cloud of ice and dust surrounding the comet, its coma, and its tail, where JWST can detect them.
When viewed spectroscopically, the water-ice in comets native to our solar system creates a strong absorption line in a comet’s spectrum at a wavelength of three microns, as well as less-prominent absorption lines at 1.5 and two microns.
Yet when the JWST’s Near-Infrared spectrograph (NIRSpec) instrument viewed 3I/ATLAS three times between August 2025, before its closest approach to the sun, and after closest approach in April 2026, scientists found the 1.5- and two micron absorption lines were missing, though the three-micron line remained strong.
"That combination was a puzzle," research lead author Silvia Protopapa of the South-west Research Institute said. "The strong three-micron band points to water-ice in the coma, but the weak or absent shorter-wavelength bands suggest the ice is not in the form we usually see in solar system comets."
The JWST's muddy 3I/ATLAS findings
Whenever presented with an unusual observational signature such the JWST delievered for 3I/ATLAS researchers turn to modeling to find the physical characteristics that best fit the spectrum. 
The modeling suggested to Protopapa’s team that 3I/ATLAS was composed of sub-micron grains of dirty water-ice, rich in dust. In comparison, the grains from the solar system’s indigenous comets are much cleaner, with almost pure water-ice relatively uncontaminated by dust.
"What seems to set [3I/ATLAS’ grains] apart is how much dust is mixed into the ice," said Protopapa. "Those grains hold clues to the conditions where the comet was born."
Comets are made of primordial material found in the planet-forming disk of gas and dust that surrounds a young star, and therefore the composition of comets can provide a window into the conditions in which planets form.
Whereas solar system comets tell us about the birth of Earth, an interstellar comet can tell us about conditions in which planets formed around another star, and how similar or dissimilar those conditions were to the birth of the solar system.
Yet comets are not the only icy remnants that date back to such primordial times. There are various families of bodies in the outer solar system, and 3I/ATLAS’ spectrum bears a resemblance to the spectrum of some medium-sized TNOs that are rich in carbon-dioxide ice and organic compounds (organic meaning containing carbon atoms). Indeed, in a separate 2025 study led by Cordiner, the JWST found 3I/ATLAS to have one of the greatest abundances of carbon dioxide ever seen in a comet.
TNOs are sizable bodies that are located far beyond the orbit of Neptune, The TNOs in question would have formed in a different part of the Sun’s protoplanetary disk than most comets and their composition reflects that.
On the other hand, the results imply that 3I/ATLAS was formed around its star of origin from similar icy material to that which produced some of the TNOs in our solar system, showing that the building blocks of planets around other stars share a common range of properties with the building blocks that formed our solar system. Indeed, 3I/ATLAS could even be a fragment of a TNO-like body that was shattered in a collision.
"At first glance, 3I/ATLAS looks different from the icy comets we know," said Protopapa. "But when we placed it alongside distant icy worlds in our own solar system, it no longer looked out of place. 
"This suggests that the icy building block of planets, here and around other stars, may share ice in the form of tiny, micron-scale grains, ranging from relatively pure ice to ice mixed with dust, with 3I/ATLAS toward the dusty end."
What this tells us is that these sub-micron-sized icy grains must form first in planet-forming disks, to then be incorporated into large bodies such as comets and protoplanets.
The team's findings were published on Monday (Oct. 26) in The Astrophysical Journal Letters.
Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

candidato.titulo: Single molecules could provide the building blocks for future quantum networks
candidato.resumo: Quantum computers rely on qubits as their units of information. To connect them into a larger network across long distances, they need to transmit quantum information using light.

texto_fonte:
Single molecules could provide the building blocks for future quantum networks
Paul Arnold
Author
Quantum computers rely on qubits as their units of information. To connect them into a larger network across long distances, they need to transmit quantum information using light.
Scientists are developing ways to do this using tiny defects in diamond crystals and other semiconductor materials that can act as qubits. However, there is a major problem. Unwanted defects and trapped electrical charges can cause fluctuations that change the frequency of light emitted by the qubits, making it harder to establish reliable quantum connections.
In new research published in the journal Nature, scientists have demonstrated a promising way to get around this instability problem by using a custom-designed molecular system that contains a stable qubit.
Building a molecular qubit
To create the qubits, a team from German startup NVision Quantum Technologies embedded a chemical compound in a crystal chosen for its ability to provide a stable environment. They then cooled the crystal to 4.5 Kelvin (around -269°C) and used laser light to convert the compound into molecules called carbenes. Each carbene molecule contains two unpaired electrons whose combined spin can be used to store quantum information.
The next step was to see whether they could control and read out the quantum state of an individual molecule. To do this, they used microwave pulses to manipulate the electrons' spin and laser light to read out the results. They also measured how long the molecules could maintain their quantum states and how stable their light emissions remained over time.
A promising breakthrough
And all this work at the molecular scale paid off.
The scientists were able to control and read out the spin state of an individual molecule and preserve the spin's delicate quantum properties for around 2.2 milliseconds.
Just as importantly, the frequencies of light emitted by individual molecules remained remarkably stable for more than one hour.
"These results establish molecular qubits as a viable platform for single-emitter quantum optics while preserving the advantages of bottom-up chemical design and processable materials," commented the study authors.
Of course, this work is only the beginning. The researchers believe their approach could eventually help develop quantum networks by allowing information stored in individual molecules to be linked to photons. The molecules could also be incorporated into thin films and integrated with existing photonic chips.
"Although the focus of this work was the demonstration of an individually addressable molecular qubit, we believe it is worth placing its properties in the broader context of the requirements for a quantum-network node."
It's a small step at the molecular scale, but potentially a big one for the future of quantum computing.

texto_fonte:
Perhaps your gaming laptop doesn’t have enough storage. Or perhaps you simply want your game library to be portable so you can move between systems. A speedy external SSD can solve both of these problems. Not only will it provide you with a lot more fast storage for your games, you can use it on any system you wish.
Choosing the external SSD that’s right for your needs means sorting through a dizzying array of protocol and speed options. Making the wrong choice could leave you disappointed, either financially or performance-wise. Luckily for you, we’ve tested a bunch of these wee beasties and can offer recommendations guaranteed to leave you satisfied.
At a glance
PROMOTION
Fortify your games and moments of glory
Built for gamers and streamers, FireCuda X Vault offers massive capacity and convenient bus-powered single-cable connectivity. Vault’s striking design with customizable RGB illumination and Windows Dynamic Lighting keeps your vibe in check and syncs to your rig’s energy.
Below are recommendations for drives from 80Gbps down to 10Gbps; scroll below those to learn more about our evaluation process and what to look for when buying an external SSD for gaming.
Note that SSD prices have risen considerably since our original reviews thanks to the AI / data center gold rush, and the recommendations below reflect that new reality. The older, linked reviews may not. We’ve also added a couple of enclosures to which you can add your own NVMe SSD, as the availability of many pre-populated SSDs is currently scattershot. Furthermore, an enclosure / DIY option is a way to save money in these time of inflated prices.
Why you should trust PCWorld for external drive reviews and buying advice: PCWorld has been putting computer hardware through its paces for decades. Our external drive evaluations are thorough and rigorous, testing the limits of every product — from performance benchmarks to the practicalities of daily use. As consumers ourselves, we know what makes a product exceptional, or not. For more about our testing process, scroll to the bottom of this article.
Samsung P9 — Best 40Gbps USB4 external SSD for gaming
Pros
- Fast and sustains long writes exceptionally well
- Runs remarkably cool despite its diminutive dimensions
- Up to 8TB of capacity
Cons
- Like all current SSDs — very expensive
Who should buy the Samsung P9?
For those who want stellar sustained throughput, but for less moolah than an 80Gbps SSD (shoot, good luck even finding one of those these days!), the Samsung P9 will get the job done and then some. Note, a 40Gbps USB4 external SSD isn’t for everyone. Your PC needs to support the USB4 or the Thunderbolt 3/4/5 spec in order to take advantage — and while cheaper than 80Gbps, it’s still not cheap.
If you’re equipped to enter the club, the Samsung P9 will reward you with nearly 4GBps transfers, and at a more affordable price than our previous pick for USB4, the Adata SE920 — which has catapulted to $556 for 1TB, compared to the P9’s MSRP of $340. Of course, with all storage right now, availability is another story. Still you can find the 2TB P9 on Amazon for $650.
Besides being very fast, the P9 is (theoretically) a good pick for anyone who wants performance and capacity, with sizes up to 8TB — again, availability being the deciding factor.
Samsung P9: Further considerations
Some other qualities that distinguish the P9 are its extremely svelte, and thus portable, size; it’s ability to maintain speed even when running very large data sets, while also remaining cool; and a nice 5-year warranty.
TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus – Best 40Gbps external SSD enclosure for gaming
Pros
- Second-fastest USB4 enclosure to date
- Solid, thermally excellent design
- Good-looking
Cons
- Bulky
Who should buy the TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus?
With the price of pre-populated 40Gbps SSDs rising due to the AI / data center memory arms race, buying a $90 (currently $76 on sale) 40Gbps enclosure such as the TerraMaster’s D1 SSD Plus, and then adding your own NVMe SSD is quite likely your most affordable external high-speed SSD option.
TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus: Further considerations
The TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus is bulky, and the style may not be everyone’s cup of tea, but the overtly finned aluminum enclosure sheds the heat inherent with faster 40Gbps SSDs extremely well.
When you populate the D1 SSD Plus, don’t overbuy with a PCIe 5.0 NVMe SSD, unless you want said SSD for use in something faster in the future. An affordable PCIe 4.0 model provides as much speed as the 40Gbps bus can handle. Note that TerraMaster also makes an 80Gbps enclosure, the D1 SSD Pro.
Read our full TerraMaster D1 SSD Plus review
PNY RP60 – Best 20Gbps external SSD for gaming
Pros
- Handsome, IP65-rated design (dust proof, water resistant)
- Good 20Gbps performance
- Nice flat Type-C USB ribbon cable
Cons
- USB port plug tether is difficult to reinsert.
Who should buy the PNY RP60?
If you tend to take your gaming drive everywhere, and/or you’re not the most careful person with hardware, a ruggedized external SSD is a practical way to ward off accidental damage.
The PNY RP60 offers more than just a rugged IP65-rated exterior that protects against dust and water droplets. It’s handsome and lightweight to boot, as well as an admirable performer, even besting one of the fastest 20Gbps drives I’ve tested — the Crucial X10 Pro — in a couple of our tests.
PNY60: Further considerations
A 20Gbps SSD is the sweet spot in the price/performance ratio for external SSDs. The only issue is that the USB 3.2×2 drives function at only 10Gbps or slower unless attached to a dedicated 20Gbps port. That applies to most USB4 and Thunderbolt ports as well.
While a sad reflection of today’s prices, the RP60 is nonetheless competitively priced at $200 and $279 for 1TB and 2TB, respectively. Note that these prices are significantly higher than when I first reviewed the RP60 due to the global NAND shortage.
Read our full PNY RP60 20Gbps USB SSD review
Asus TUF Gaming A2 – Best 20Gbps external SSD enclosure for gaming
Pros
- Very fast performer
- Military-esque styling
- Super-rugged IP68 rated
- Affordable
Cons
- You need to provide the NVMe SSD
- Requires a USB 3.2×2 port for 20Gbps performance
Who should buy the Asus TUF Gaming A2?
Many gamers build their own gaming rig, so why shouldn’t they roll their own external SSD with an affordable enclosure such as the $60 TUF Gaming A2? With the price of pre-populated external SSDs currently reaching for the stratosphere, it’s an especially attractive proposition for 2026.
The TUF Gaming A2 is styled to appeal to gamers, especially fans of first-person, military-style shooters. It’s built like a tank, carries an IP68 rating, and is easy to open for installing your NVMe SSD.
Asus TUF Gaming A2: Further considerations
The TUF Gaming A2 allows you to leverage older NVMe SSDs. Even a PCIe 3.0 SSD is fast enough for the 20Gbps bus, if you find a deal. With those going the way of the Dodo, however, an affordable PCIe 4.0 model will do just fine.
Read our full Asus TUF Gaming A2 review
Corsair EX300U – Best 10Gbps external SSD for gaming
Pros
- Fastest 10Gbps SSD we’ve tested
- Small profile
- Magnetic attachement to metal surfaces
Cons
- Almost as pricey as 20Gbps SSDs currently
Who should buy the Corsair EX300U?
For those looking for an SSD that won’t break the bank, but is still “fast enough,” the EX300U is an appealing little magnetic square of a drive. That said, $175 for 1TB is almost as pricey as the 20Gbps PNY RP60 listed above. Formerly, the drive was $100 at that capacity.
Scant savings aside, the EX300U is the fastest 10Gbps SSD I’ve tested to date, besting the Teamgroup X2 Max listed below by a small margin. And unlike the latter, you can stick it to a metal object like a PC case via the circular magnet on the back. Note that aluminum is not particularly magnetic, so this doesn’t work with most Macs.
Corsair EX300U: Further considerations
The warranty on the EX300U is three years, which is the usual for external SSDs, but the 250TBW (terabytes that can be written) per terabyte of capacity is a little stingy. At least Corsair provides a TBW rating — most vendors don’t for external SSDs.
Still, the odds of anyone exceeding that TBW limit is rather low. Most of the time games are reading data, not writing it.
Read our full Corsair EX300U review
Teamgroup X2 Max — Best 10Gbps thumb drive SSD for gaming
Pros
- Svelte thumb drive form factor
- Fastest 10Gbps SSD we’ve tested
- Dual Type-A/Type-C connectors
Cons
- End caps aren’t captive
Who should buy the Teamgroup X2 Max?
For those who want both fast 10Gbps performance, plus the super convenience of the thumb drive form factor and both Type-A and Type-C connectivity, it doesn’t get any better than the X2 Max. In fact, it’s the second-fastest 10Gbps SSD of any type that I’ve tested. Right behind the Corsair EX300U shown above.
While it may not be sexy-looking in the gaming sense, pulling this out of your pocket when you sit down to game is the ultimate sandbag move. Let them laugh, they’ll never see you coming.
Having both Type-A and Type-C connectors on board means never having to worry about what type of computer you’ll be using the X2 Max on, though having a thumb drive attached to your laptop can be a bit awkward if you’re lounging on the couch, etc.
Teamgroup X2 Max: Further considerations
While some gamers might scoff at “only” 10Gbps, that’s still plenty fast enough for loading games — and seek times are roughly the same as 80/40/20Gbps SSDs. Where you’ll lose out a bit compared to those faster models is in the time it takes saving games in the first place.
Note that the 2TB X2 Max was on target for a 10Gbps SSD writing our 450GB file, never slowing appreciably or tragically as some do. The 1TB might not do quite as well.
The current pricing of *cough* $330 for the 2TB model means you should weigh this option against faster options for a little more cash, and/or creating your own external SSD using the enclosures listed above. A roll-your-own model, however, will never be this portable.
Read our full Teamgroup X2 Max review
Other notable external SSDs for gaming
- Orico TB5 dock: For anyone looking to add extra ports to their PC and an M.2 NVMe slot for super-fast Thunderbolt 5 storage, this dock does it, for a price.
- Asus ROG Strix Aiolos: This 20Gbps NVMe enclosure offers RGB lighting and easy access to the internal M.2 slot.
- Asus PA40SU: A good-performing single NVMe, USB4 drive enclosure that makes DIY storage easy, and looks nice in the process.
- Glyph Atom EX20: Comes in a good-looking, protective silicon jacket while offering speedy 20Gbps performance.
- Glyph Atom EX40: Sibling to the above, it has a similar sturdy exterior combined with USB4 compatibility and 40Gbps speed.
- MSI DataMag 40Gbps: Not the fastest USB4 drive, but it’s got magnetic mounting.
- Teamgroup PD20: A handsome, tough, and decently fast 20Gbps drive.
- Crucial X10: A tiny, weatherproofed drive that can hold up to 8TB of storage.
- Sandisk Extreme Pro SSD with USB4: A handsome design and relative affordability, but connection issues and comparably lackluster 40Gbps performance left us unamazed.
- Addlink P21: Has a compelling combination of good performance and a striking design.
- Corsair EX400U: On the slow side for a USB4 external SSD, but can sometimes be less expensive than the competition.
- Seagate Game Drive SSD: Targeted at PS4/PS5 owners, this 10Gbps SSD is very fast for its class as well as attractively styled, complete with a Playstation logo, though it’s relatively pricey.
- Lexar Armor 700: A 20Gbps drive that can withstand some abuse — perfect for the gamer on the go or the accident-prone.
- Adata SD810: A solid 20Gbps drive, save for writing large amounts of data, where it slows down.
How PCWorld tests external drives
Drive tests currently utilize Windows 11 24H2, 64-bit running off of a PCIe 4.0 Samsung 990 Pro in an Asus Z890-Creator WiFi (PCIe 4.0/5.0) motherboard. The CPU is a Core Ultra i5 225 feeding/fed by two Crucial 64GB DDR5 5600MHz modules (128GB of memory total).
Both 20Gbps USB and Thunderbolt 5 are integrated into the motherboard and Intel CPU/GPU graphics are used. Internal PCIe 5.0 SSDs involved in testing are mounted in an Asus Hyper M.2 x16 Gen5 adapter card sitting in a PCIe 5.0 slot.
We run the CrystalDiskMark 8.04 (and 9), AS SSD 2, and ATTO 4 synthetic benchmarks (to keep article length down, we report only the first) to find the storage device’s potential performance. Then we run a series of 48GB transfer and 450GB write tests using Windows Explorer drag and drop to show what users will see during routine copy operations, as well as the far speedier FastCopy run as administrator to show what’s possible.
A 25GBps two-SSD RAID 0 array on the aforementioned Asus Hyper M.2 x16 Gen5 is used as the second drive in our transfer tests. Formerly the 48GB tests were done with a RAM disk serving that purpose.
Each test is performed on a NTFS-formatted and newly TRIM’d drive so the results are optimal. Note that in normal use, as a drive fills up, performance may decrease due to less NAND for secondary caching, as well as other factors. This issue has abated somewhat with the current crop of SSDs utilizing more mature controllers and far faster, late-generation NAND.
Caveat: The performance numbers shown apply only to the drive we were shipped and to the capacity tested. SSD performance can and will vary by capacity due to more or fewer chips to shotgun reads/writes across and the amount of NAND available for secondary caching. Vendors also occasionally swap components. If you ever notice a large discrepancy between the performance you experience and that which we report, by all means, let us know.
Note also that some of the SSDs in this roundup were tested using other equipment and methodologies, which you can read about in the standalone reviews.
To learn more about our testing methodology see PCWorld’s article on how we test external SSDs.
Who curated this article?
Having started computing by flipping switches, Jon L. Jacobi has witnessed storage morph from punch cards and tape to solid state. He’s been using and testing HDDs, SATA SSDs, and NVMe SSDs for PCWorld for well over two decades. To paraphrase a well-known commercial, you might say he’s seen a thing or two.
FAQ
What is the best external SSD for gaming?
At 80Gbps, the LaCie Rugged SSD Pro5 is our choice for absolute best performance. If speed is important, but you want to save a bit of coin, then the best 40Gbps external drive is the Adata SE920. For still-great 20Gbps performance, and a significant cost savings, consider the PNY RP60 and Crucial X10 Pro. Note that the Teamgroup X2 Max still offers good 10Gbps in a super-small form factor.
What are the speeds of the various external interfaces and which one do you want?
In descending order of performance the current external interfaces are: 80Gbps Thunderbolt 5/USB4, 40Gbps USB4/Thunderbolt 3 and 4, 20Gbps USB 3.2×2 (dedicated port required or it’s 10Gbps), 10GBps USB 3.2, then 5Gbps USB 3.x. For optimal gaming performance, we recommend 20Gbps or higher, though you can easily make do with 10Gbps.
Note that currently, the real-world difference in performance between 40Gbps and 80Gbps is minimal. Also, the increase in power draw and heat produced as you climb the performance ladder from 10Gbps to 80Gbps is noticeable.
Note that you’ll occasionally see mentions of 120Gbps Thunderbolt 5. 120Gbps is only available for downstream video, not storage or other applications. 80Gbps is the current top of the line.
What causes an external SSD to fail?
While mechanical hard drives are much more prone to failure than SSDs, it is still possible for an SSD to give up the ghost. Generally it’s the result of a controller failure, although that’s an increasingly rare occurrence; it’s also a relatively easy fix/reset for someone who knows the SSD’s internals such as a recovery service.
SSDs will also eventually wear out, though this only precludes further writing to the unit. You can still read what’s on the drive, so it’s not the disaster a HDD failure can be. There were also instances in the ancient past of static electricity bricking Type-A connected SSDs upon insertion.
Why does Windows say my external drive has less capacity than specified?
This discrepancy is due to the difference between the binary and decimal number systems, their nomenclatures, and a Microsoft miscue. Your 2TB drive indeed has 2 trillion bytes of storage, and if you look at the byte count that Windows displays in a drive’s properties dialog, this should be what you see. This, in the International System of Units (SI/decimal), is 2 terabytes, or 2TB. Vendors use this system as consumers are far more familiar with base 10 than binary.
However, Windows uses the newer International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) binary multiples such as 2^10 (Kibibyte/KiB), 2^20 (Mebibyte/MiB), 2^30 (Gibibyte/Gib), etc. Binary multiples are larger than their decimal near-equivalents (one KiB is 1,024 bytes, one MiB is 1,048,576 bytes) so when Windows divides the total bytes by the IEC values you get something like 1.8TiB for a 2TB drive. Alas, Windows labels this as 1.8TB rather than 1.8TiB, misleading the user.
Other reasons you might not see as much available storage in the properties tab are formatting or partitioning. The file system uses some storage for file location and size info, etc. Also, some drives come with a small partition containing software so the main partition will be smaller than the drive’s total capacity.
How long will my external SSD last?
SSDs don’t wear out or break mechanically like a hard drive, but their cells can only be written to so many times. SSDs generally have a TBW (terabytes that may be written) rating, but this is rarely provided by vendors for external SSDs. Hint: They may not use the same SSD inside throughout the product lifespan.
Most internal M.2 NVMe TLC SSDs are rated for around 600TBW per terabyte, and QLC types for around 200TBW, though the type of NAND in use is also rarely provided by vendors. That’s a lot of data, and a lot of SSDs are rated well below what they might actually achieve. You can guesstimate by using a utility to see how much data you write to an SSD a day and then doing the math.
External SSD warranties are generally between three and five years. As with all such things, it’s a financial risk formula calculated by the company. In this case based on expected NAND longevity and price. As is the TBW rating. Our best guess based on experience is perhaps a decade. However, certain models have had issues long before that — generally due to a flaw or failure in the bridge chip or controller.
Exceeding a SSD’s rating does not affect the data stored on it. You can still read that data, you just can’t write more of it to the drive.
Should you build your own external SSD with an enclosure and an NVMe SSD?
Due to the current high price of NAND, buying an enclosure and populating it with an NVMe SSD is a more enticing proposition than ever before, and it has always appealed to PC builders. Note that even a PCIe 3.0 NVMe SSD will give you good performance in up to 20Gbps enclosures, though you’ll need at least a PCIe 4.0 model to get the most out of an 40/80Gbps enclosure.

texto_fonte:
A recent scroll through social media got me thinking about trust. About half my feed was filled with AI slop that astute users would call out as being machine-generated, often to the embarrassment of the rube who unknowingly spread it and sometimes to the delight of the poster who shared it deliberately because they found it amusing or useful for sowing confusion.
Remember the good old days of GPT-3 when we could ask the chatbot anything and it would almost instantly and very confidently spit back a plausible but false answer? That’s when the word “hallucination” as applied to AI answers entered the lexicon. Six years and several versions of a few different chatbots later, I still can’t trust the answers I get, even though Claude or Gemini often do useful work for me. That’s the thing about current AI: Trust but verify. And verify you must.
Apply that maxim at scale to maintain the integrity of the scientific record and you get an idea of the challenge facing publishers of peer-reviewed scholarship. In “I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper,” freelance writer and doctor of applied mathematics Benjamin Skuse tells the story of the human gatekeepers trying to beat back the rising tide of AI slop by attempting to get his own AI-generated papers past IEEE’s defenses.
“He basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper.’ And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it.” —Eliza Strickland
As features and AI beat editor Eliza Strickland told me, Skuse was surprised at just how effortless it was to generate a paper that was more or less plausible and more or less science. For one of his experiments, “he basically hit ‘run experiment’ and ‘write paper,’” she said. “And then he didn’t do a damn thing to it. He just launched it into the maw of the publishing engine.”
Skuse discovered that the combination of IEEE’s human-review processes and research-integrity checker programs are currently keeping pace in what amounts to a cat-and-mouse game against people using free tools. But the more advanced LLMs are no longer making the same dumb mistakes the free versions do. That leaves publishers locked in an arms race between increasingly plausible slop and the systems aimed at detecting it.
Scholarly publishers aren’t the only ones trying to hold the line against slop. So is that global depository of human-generated knowledge, Wikipedia. For this month’s Five Questions, Strickland interviewed Ellia Lebleu, a founding member of WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort to detect and delete AI-generated material from the platform. Lebleu’s team is confronting the same problem as commercial publishers, but with fewer people and fewer tools.
“Wikipedia is known as a repository of human-generated information, and they want to hold on to that,” says Strickland. “Who knows how long they’ll be able to do that.”
If we can’t collectively assume that the scientific record is trustworthy or that basic facts about the world are accurate, then our understanding of what is real unspools into uncertainty. Perhaps that delights quantum scientists and the grifters who thrive in an information environment where there is no shared reality. But that uncertainty ultimately undermines trust in the institutions that exist to curate the corpus of human knowledge and to promote the advancement of science and technology for the benefit of humanity.
Or maybe in a world where AI is doing the science and writing the papers, it won’t matter whether or not humans trust the outputs. As Strickland put it, “Doesn’t it just feel crazy that we’ll have AI writing for other AIs at some point? We’ll just get left out of the loop.”
- How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written ›
- AI Boosts Research Careers but Flattens Scientific Discovery ›
- I Used AI to Fake a Scientific Paper. Here’s What Happened ›

candidato.titulo: Robot platform combines AI and rapid imaging to improve perovskite solar cell fabrication
candidato.resumo: Solar cells generate electricity by absorbing sunlight in a thin layer of perovskite, a light-absorbing material. This layer is made with a liquid solution that dries and crystallizes into a solid film, but small changes in temperature, humidity and other conditions can affect the film and the performance of the solar cell.

texto_fonte:
Robot platform combines AI and rapid imaging to improve perovskite solar cell fabrication
Solar cells generate electricity by absorbing sunlight in a thin layer of perovskite, a light-absorbing material. This layer is made with a liquid solution that dries and crystallizes into a solid film, but small changes in temperature, humidity and other conditions can affect the film and the performance of the solar cell.
Now, recent research combining a robot system with machine learning may overcome this challenge. Researchers from the University of Osaka have published their findings on a newly developed automated platform for fabricating perovskite films. The system coordinates film deposition with optical imaging and environmental measurements. The findings were published in ACS Nano.
The team used the platform to investigate the transformation of the liquid coating to a crystalline film, focusing on changes in film color and the behavior of antisolvent droplets. As these changes can occur rapidly, the researchers needed measurements that could capture the process on very short timescales. The resulting observations provided detailed information about how events during film formation influence the final material.
"We want to move beyond trial and error by measuring what happens to the film while it is actually forming," says lead author Ryosuke Kado. "Our system allows us to connect these real-time changes with the quality of the perovskite film and identify the factors that matter most."
Tracking droplets within milliseconds
The system can capture changes in film color on a subsecond timescale and resolve the motion and impact of antisolvent droplets within just a few milliseconds. By capturing these rapid events, the platform enabled the researchers to examine how the timing and behavior of the droplets influence subsequent film formation.
"The advantage of automation is that we can collect much richer information than would be practical by hand," says senior author Akinori Saeki. "Machine learning helps us make sense of these many variables and identify relationships that are difficult to see."
Droplet control improves solar-cell efficiency
The researchers also applied these insights to refine the antisolvent coating process. The analysis identified an optimal range for droplet behavior, which the researchers used to guide the fabrication of a lead-based perovskite solar-cell device.
Under the optimized conditions, the device reached a power conversion efficiency of 24.4%, demonstrating that information gathered during film formation could be used to improve an actual solar cell.
By enabling researchers to observe and analyze film formation as it happens, the platform offers a more systematic approach to optimizing solar-cell fabrication. The combination of automated experimentation, real-time measurements and data analysis could help uncover previously unknown relationships between processing conditions and film quality. The team is optimistic that this technology will catalyze photovoltaic research and enable more practical solar cells.
Publication details
Ryosuke Kado et al., Automated Perovskite Film Fabrication with High-Resolution Data Acquisition and Machine Learning Analysis, ACS Nano (2026). DOI: 10.1021/acsnano.6c11386

candidato.titulo: Mercado Bitcoin pode ter perdido R$ 217 milhões em ataque hacker
candidato.resumo: Corretora brasileira afirma que clientes não tiveram prejuízos nem dados vazados. Depósitos e saques foram temporariamente suspensos. Mercado Bitcoin pode ter perdido R$ 217 milhões em ataque hacker

texto_fonte:
Mercado Bitcoin identificou e conteve um incidente de segurança em um de seus sistemas.
O incidente teria envolvido cerca de US$ 40 milhões, mas a empresa afirma que não houve prejuízos aos clientes nem vazamento de dados.
A corretora está investigando o caso com a ajuda das autoridades e manterá atualizações regulares sobre o andamento da situação.
A Mercado Bitcoin, uma das maiores corretoras de ativos digitais do Brasil, informou nesta segunda-feira (02/11) que identificou e conteve um incidente de segurança em um de seus sistemas. Como medida preventiva, a empresa suspendeu temporariamente os serviços de depósito e saque.
O alerta sobre possíveis movimentações irregulares partiu da Hypernative, empresa especializada em segurança de blockchain. Segundo o monitoramento, cerca de US$ 40 milhões (aproximadamente R$ 217,7 milhões) teriam sido transferidos de carteiras ligadas à corretora.
Comunicado oficial:
Identificamos e contivemos com rapidez um incidente de segurança em um de nossos sistemas nesta madrugada.
Reforçamos que:
• Não houve nenhum prejuízo aos clientes;
• Não houve vazamento de dados.
Como medida preventiva de proteção, depósitos e saques estão temporariamente suspensos. Nossas equipes estão mobilizadas investigando o caso, rastreando os ativos e coordenando as medidas junto às autoridades competentes.
Manteremos atualizações regulares por aqui.
A maior parte das transferências teria acontecido entre 3h19 e 3h53 de hoje, no horário de Brasília. Os ativos foram enviados para endereços recém-criados, associados pela empresa de segurança a um possível invasor.
Em comunicado, a Mercado Bitcoin afirmou que identificou e conteve o problema, sem prejuízos aos clientes ou vazamento de dados. A corretora, porém, não confirmou o valor estimado pela Hypernative, mas está investigando o caso junto às autoridades.
Binance sofreu roubo histórico há poucos dias
O incidente ocorre poucos dias após a Binance registrar o que foi apontado como o maior roubo de criptomoedas da história. Na sexta-feira (30/10), a principal corretora do mercado informou que uma invasão movimentou cerca de US$ 6,3 bilhões (R$ 33,9 bilhões) em ativos de carteiras de clientes.
A investigação inicial da Binance indica que os invasores podem ter acessado o notebook de um engenheiro de DevOps, profissional que atua na integração entre desenvolvimento e operações. A partir do computador, os hackers teriam conseguido entrar em serviços internos da corretora usando os privilégios de acesso do funcionário.
A Binance afirmou que vai cobrir integralmente os prejuízos causados pelo ataque. Na ocasião, a empresa também suspendeu depósitos e saques enquanto investigava o incidente e analisava seus sistemas. Os depósitos já foram retomados.
Bruno Andrade é jornalista formado pela Universidade Estadual Paulista (Unesp) e técnico em eletrônica. Antes de se juntar ao Tecnoblog, trabalhou na reportagem e na edição de homepage do portal iG. Tem experiência como redator, repórter e editor.
